title: A Flat by the River
body:
Last spring, Priya Sharma got a job offer from a design company in Glasgow. She was twenty-seven and had always lived in Leicester, near her parents. At first she wasn't sure. Glasgow was almost three hundred miles away, and she didn't know anybody there. But the job was better than her old one, and the salary was higher too. In the end, she said yes.

The first weeks were hard. She stayed in a cheap guest house while she looked for a flat. It rained almost every day, and rents in the centre were high. She viewed seven flats in two weeks. One was too dark, one was above a noisy pub, and one had a kitchen the size of a cupboard.

Finally, she found a bright one-bedroom flat in the West End, near the River Kelvin. The landlord, a friendly retired teacher called Mr Duncan, left her a box of shortbread and a note: “Welcome to Glasgow!”

At first, Priya felt lonely in the evenings. She missed her mum's cooking and her old friends. Then her colleagues invited her to a ceilidh, a Scottish dance night. She was terrible at the dances, but she laughed all evening.

Now, a year later, she has never been happier. “I still miss Leicester,” she says, “but Glasgow feels like home.”

title: Day One with the Wrong Spanner
body:
Last September, I started a plumbing apprenticeship with a small company in Salford, near Manchester. I was seventeen. Most of my friends from school went to sixth form, but I didn't want to sit in a classroom all day. I wanted to work with my hands and earn some money.

On my first morning, my alarm went off at six. I was so nervous that I couldn't eat breakfast. My boss, Denise, picked me up in her van at seven. She has been a plumber for twenty-five years, and she explained everything slowly and clearly.

Our first job was a leaking pipe under a kitchen sink in an old terraced house. Denise did the work, and I passed her the tools. Well, I tried to. I gave her the wrong spanner three times! She just laughed and said, “Don't worry, everybody does that on day one.”

In the afternoon, we fitted a new shower in a flat. I carried the heavy boxes up the stairs and watched her carefully. By five o'clock, I was tired, dirty and very happy.

Now I work four days a week with Denise and spend one day at college. The course is harder than I thought, but I'm learning a lot every week. In three years, I'm going to be a qualified plumber.

title: Thirty Under the Fig Trees
body:
For her thirtieth birthday, Mia Nguyen didn't want a big night out. “Bars are too loud and too expensive,” she told her flatmate, Jess. “I'm going to have a picnic in the park instead.”

She chose a Sunday in March, when Sydney is still warm but not too hot. She sent a message to twenty friends: “Centennial Park, 12 o'clock, near the big fig trees. Bring a blanket and something to share. No presents, please!”

On Saturday evening, Mia and Jess made rice paper rolls and a huge pavlova. Jess also bought a bag of balloons and twenty paper cups.

The next day, the sky was clear and blue. Friends arrived with sausage rolls, fruit, salads and homemade lamingtons. Mia's dad brought a portable barbecue and cooked sausages for everyone. Someone played music, and a few of the children started a game of cricket on the grass.

At about four o'clock, dark clouds came over the park. Ten minutes later, it was pouring. Everyone grabbed their food and ran under the trees, laughing and screaming. The pavlova didn't survive, but nobody cared.

“This was the best birthday I've ever had,” Mia said that evening, wet but smiling. “Next year, I'm doing it again.”

title: Minus Thirty
body:
When Lucas Oliveira arrived in Winnipeg from São Paulo in August, the weather was warm and sunny. He walked to his university classes in a T-shirt and thought, “Canadian winters can't be that bad.”

He was wrong. By the end of October, there was frost on the cars every morning. In November, the first snow fell. Lucas wore his thickest hoodie and a light rain jacket, but he was still freezing. His classmate Hannah looked at him and shook her head. “You need a real winter coat,” she said. “In January, it's going to be minus thirty.”

That Saturday, they took the bus to an outdoor clothing store. Lucas was surprised by the prices. The warmest parkas cost more than four hundred dollars. He tried on six different jackets. Some were too long, and others were too tight across the shoulders. Finally, he found a dark green parka with a fur-lined hood. It wasn't the cheapest, but it was on sale for thirty percent off.

Hannah also helped him choose a toque, thick mittens and warm boots. “Never buy cheap boots,” she told him. “Your feet will thank you.”

In January, the temperature really did drop to minus thirty-two. Lucas walked to class, warm and comfortable, and realized that Hannah was right.

title: Back in the Water
body:
Last winter, Marcus Bell had terrible back pain. He was forty-four, he worked in an office in Chicago, and he sat at his desk for nine hours a day. Some mornings, he couldn't even bend down to tie his shoes.

His doctor examined him and said, “There's nothing seriously wrong, but the muscles in your back are weak. You need to move more. Swimming is one of the best things for your back.”

Marcus hadn't swum since high school. He was a little embarrassed, but he signed up for an adult swim club at his local YMCA. The group met three evenings a week, at six thirty.

The first session was hard. The other swimmers were faster and fitter than he was, and after four lengths he was out of breath. The coach, a cheerful woman named Rosa, put him in the slowest lane and gave him a kickboard. “Everybody starts somewhere,” she said with a smile.

Marcus kept going. After a month, he could swim twenty lengths without stopping. After three months, his back pain was almost gone. He also made new friends. On Fridays after practice, the group often went out for tacos together.

Now Marcus swims four times a week. “I've never felt better,” he says. “Why didn't I start years ago?”

title: Aoife's Week on the Sofa
body:
Monday, 13 January
I woke up this morning with a sore throat and a blocked nose. I went to work anyway because we had an important meeting. Big mistake. By lunchtime, I was sneezing every two minutes and my colleagues were moving their chairs away from me. My manager, Declan, sent me home at three.

Tuesday
I felt even worse today. My head was heavy, and I had a temperature of 38.2. I rang the office and said I was staying at home. I spent the whole day on the sofa under a blanket, watching old episodes of a baking show. I wasn't hungry at all.

Wednesday
Mam came over with a big pot of chicken soup and a bag of oranges. She also made me a hot whiskey with honey, lemon and cloves, an old Irish cure. “It never fails,” she said. I'm not sure it worked, but I slept for ten hours.

Thursday
Much better! My temperature was normal again, and I was finally hungry. I ate two bowls of soup and some toast. I still had a cough, so I didn't go out.

Friday
Back to work today. Declan asked me how I was. “Grand,” I said. Next time I'm sick, I'm going to stay at home from the first day.

title: Four Seasons in One Week
body:
Every summer, the Okafor family from Birmingham goes on holiday to the seaside. Last August, they rented a small cottage in St Ives, in Cornwall, for a week.

On the first day, the weather was perfect. The sun was shining, and the sea was a beautiful turquoise colour. Ada and her younger brother, Tobi, built sandcastles on the beach while their parents read under a big umbrella. In the evening, they ate fish and chips by the harbour. A seagull stole one of Dad's chips, and everyone laughed except Dad.

On Tuesday, it was cloudy and windy. They went for a long walk along the coast path and watched the surfers in the big waves. On Wednesday and Thursday, it rained all day. The children were bored in the cottage, so Mum took them to an aquarium in Newquay, and in the evening Dad taught them a new card game.

On Friday, there was thick fog in the morning, but by lunchtime the sun was out again. The family went back to the beach and then had a cream tea in a little café: scones with jam and clotted cream.

“The weather was so changeable,” said Mum on the long drive home. “It was like four seasons in one week.”

“Can we come back next year?” asked Tobi. Everyone said yes.

title: Cracked
body:
Last Tuesday, Jasmine Torres was running for the bus in Austin when her phone slipped out of her hand. It fell onto the sidewalk, screen first. When she picked it up, her heart sank. The screen was covered in cracks, like a spider web.

The phone still worked, but it was hard to read anything. When she typed a message, tiny pieces of glass came off on her finger. “I can't use it like this,” she thought.

That evening, she looked online. A new phone was going to cost almost nine hundred dollars, and her old one was only eighteen months old. Her roommate, Kayla, told her about a small repair shop near the university. “They fixed my laptop last year,” she said. “They're fast and cheap.”

The next morning, Jasmine took her phone to the shop. The technician, an older man named Mr. Patel, looked at it carefully. “The screen is broken, but the inside is fine,” he said. “I can replace the screen for a hundred and twenty dollars. Come back in two hours.”

Jasmine went to a coffee shop down the street and read a book. When she came back, her phone looked brand-new.

That afternoon, she bought a strong case and a screen protector. “I've learned my lesson,” she said.

title: Wednesday Nights in the Kitchen
body:
Sione Taufa is a bus driver in Wellington. For years, his dinner was always the same: toast, instant noodles or takeaway fish and chips. When his doctor told him to eat more vegetables, he decided it was time to learn to cook.

In February, he signed up for an evening cooking course at the local high school. Many schools in New Zealand run night classes for adults. The course was called “Easy Thai Cooking” and cost one hundred and sixty dollars for eight weeks.

On the first Wednesday, Sione was nervous. There were eleven other students: some young couples, a retired nurse and two university students. The teacher, Nok, came from Chiang Mai. She showed them how to chop garlic, ginger and chillies quickly and safely. Then everyone made a green curry with chicken and fresh basil.

Sione's curry was much too spicy. He used five chillies instead of one, and his eyes were watering for ten minutes. Everyone laughed, including Sione.

Week by week, he got better. He learned to make pad thai, spring rolls and mango sticky rice. On the last evening, the students cooked a big dinner together and invited their families.

Now Sione cooks at home four nights a week. “Before the course, my kitchen was the cleanest room in the house,” he jokes. “Now it's the busiest.”

title: Dear Grandma
body:
Dear Grandma,

Thank you so much for the package! It arrived on Thursday, right in the middle of my final exams. When I saw your handwriting on the box, I smiled for the first time all week.

The cookies were amazing. I shared some with my roommate, Ava, but I hid the rest under my bed. She doesn't know about them! They tasted exactly like the ones you made when I was little and stayed at your house every summer.

I also love the scarf. Did you really knit it yourself? The color is perfect. Philadelphia is much colder than I expected this month, so I wear it every day. Two people at the library have already asked me where I bought it.

And thank you for the twenty dollars. You didn't have to do that! I'm going to take Ava out for pizza after our last exam.

My exams finish on December 15th, and I'm going to fly home on the 18th. Mom says we're all going to drive up to Minnesota for Christmas. I can't wait to see you and Grandpa. Can we bake cookies together again?

Lots of love,
Zoe

P.S. Please give Biscuit a big hug from me and tell him I'm bringing him a new toy.

title: A Ute for the Country
body:
In June, Hamish Wright got his first job as a vet nurse at an animal clinic near Horsham, in country Victoria. He was excited, but there was one problem. He lived in Melbourne and had never owned a car. In the city, he took the tram everywhere. Near Horsham, the farms were far apart and there was almost no public transport.

His budget was fifteen thousand dollars. On Saturday, he went to a used car dealer with his uncle Rob, who knows a lot about cars. The salesman showed them a shiny red sports car first. “Too small, and the insurance is too expensive,” said Rob.

Then they looked at a white ute. It was eight years old and had 120,000 kilometres on the clock, but it was in good condition. There was space in the back for animal food and equipment. Rob checked the tyres and the engine and took it for a test drive.

“It's a good one,” he said quietly. “But don't pay the full price.”

The price was $16,500. Hamish was nervous, but he asked for a discount. In the end, the salesman agreed to $14,800, with six months' rego included.

Two weeks later, Hamish drove to his new job. On his first morning, he helped a farmer with a sick sheep.

title: Enough Was Enough
body:
Olivia Chen hadn't had a haircut for more than a year. First she was too busy at work, then she moved house, and then she just forgot. Her long black hair now reached the middle of her back, and the ends were dry and split. One morning, her hairbrush got stuck, and she decided enough was enough.

That afternoon, she booked an appointment at a small salon near her flat in Hackney. The hairdresser, Kemi, ran her fingers through Olivia's hair and laughed kindly.

“When did you last come in?” she asked.
“Last spring, I think,” said Olivia. “Maybe the spring before.”
“So, what would you like today? Just a trim?”
Olivia showed her a photo on her phone. “Actually, I'd like something completely different. Shoulder length, with a fringe.”
“Are you sure? That's a big change.”
“I'm sure. It's time.”

Kemi washed Olivia's hair and started cutting. Long pieces of hair fell onto the floor. Olivia closed her eyes. Forty minutes later, Kemi turned the chair towards the mirror.

Olivia couldn't believe it. She looked younger and fresher, and her head felt light.

The haircut cost fifty-five pounds, and she left a tip. Before she went home, she booked her next appointment for eight weeks later. “I'm not waiting a year again,” she promised.

title: Twenty-Five Years on Broadway
body:
Robert and Linda Kowalski live in a small town in New Jersey. Last October, they celebrated their twenty-fifth wedding anniversary. Their daughter, Megan, gave them a surprise present: two tickets for a Broadway musical in New York City.

Linda was thrilled. She loved musicals, but they hadn't been to the theater since before Megan was born. Robert was less excited. “Three hours of singing?” he said. “I'm going to fall asleep.”

On the evening of the show, Linda wore a dark blue dress, and Robert put on the suit from Megan's graduation. They took the train into Manhattan and had dinner at an Italian restaurant near Times Square. The streets were full of bright lights and tourists taking photos.

The theater was old and beautiful, with red velvet seats and gold decorations on the ceiling. Their seats were in the balcony, but they could see the stage perfectly. When the lights went down and the orchestra started playing, Linda held Robert's hand.

Robert didn't fall asleep. In fact, he laughed at all the jokes, and in the second act he even cried a little. At the end, the whole audience stood up and clapped for five minutes.

On the train home, Robert was quiet for a long time. Then he said, “So, what are we going to see next year?”

title: Ten Days Before Lisbon
body:
In early May, Arjun Mehta was packing for a two-week holiday in Portugal with his girlfriend, Chloé. He was looking for his passport when he noticed the date on it. It expired in March. Their flight from Toronto was in ten days.

Arjun panicked. He went online and read about passport renewals. A normal renewal by mail takes about twenty business days. That was too slow. But there was another option: if you can show proof of travel, you can apply in person at a passport office and pay extra for faster service.

The next morning, he took the day off work and went to the passport office downtown. He brought his old passport, two new photos, the application form and a copy of his flight booking. The lineup was already long at eight thirty, so he waited for almost two hours.

title: Fifteen Years Later
body:
On Saturday morning, Amira Hussain was buying a birthday card in a shop on Briggate, in the centre of Leeds. When she turned around, she nearly walked into a tall woman with short red hair and a pushchair.

“Sorry!” said Amira. Then she stopped. “Wait... Rachel? Rachel Thompson?”

The woman stared at her. “Amira? From Roundhay High? I don't believe it!”

They hugged in the middle of the shop. The last time they saw each other was at their leaving party, fifteen years ago. At school, they were best friends. They sat next to each other in every class and spent every weekend together. But after their A levels, Amira went to university in London, Rachel moved to Newcastle for work, and slowly they lost touch.

They went to a café nearby and talked for two hours. Rachel was a paramedic now and had moved back to Leeds last year. The baby in the pushchair was her son, Alfie. Amira worked as an accountant and had a seven-year-old daughter.

“Do you remember Mr Hughes, the chemistry teacher?” laughed Rachel. “And the time we set fire to the lab?”

“It was a very small fire!” said Amira.

Before they said goodbye, they swapped phone numbers. “Let's not wait another fifteen years,” said Rachel. They're meeting again next Friday.

title: Which Way to the Museum?
body:
Yuki Tanaka was on holiday in Edinburgh for three days. After a morning at the castle, she wanted to see the National Museum of Scotland. Her phone battery was dead, and she had no paper map, so she decided to ask people.

First, she asked a man in a kilt who was playing the bagpipes on the Royal Mile. He pointed down the hill. “Go that way, hen. It's not far.” Yuki didn't know what “hen” meant, but she thanked him and walked on.

After five minutes, she wasn't sure. She asked a young couple with a big map. “Sorry,” they said. “We're tourists too. We're from Spain!”

Next, she asked an older woman with a dog. “The museum? Oh, that's easy,” said the woman. “Go straight on and take the third street on the left.” Yuki followed her directions, but she ended up at a supermarket.

Finally, she went into a small bookshop and asked the man at the counter. He drew her a little map. “Go back to the Royal Mile and turn right onto George IV Bridge. Then take the first left, and you're on Chambers Street. The museum is the big building on your right. You can't miss it.”

Ten minutes later, Yuki was standing in front of the museum. It was free, and it was wonderful. She stayed there until it closed.

title: Saturdays in Montgomery Square
body:
Every Saturday for thirty years, Margaret Wilson has done the same thing. She wakes up at six, makes a cup of tea, and takes her old blue shopping trolley out of the cupboard. At eight o'clock, she walks to the Saturday market in Montgomery Square, in the centre of Nelson.

Margaret first went to the market in 1995, when she moved to Nelson with her husband, Bill. They had two small children and not much money. “The vegetables were cheaper than at the supermarket,” she remembers, “and much fresher.”

Bill died six years ago, but Margaret still follows the same route around the stalls. First, she buys free-range eggs from a young farmer called Aroha. Then she gets apples and kiwifruit from the Patel family, who have had their orchard for three generations. After that, she chooses a loaf of sourdough at the bakery stall and a small piece of local cheese.

Her last stop is always the coffee cart. The owner, Finn, starts making her flat white when he sees her trolley. She sits on a bench, drinks her coffee and chats with old friends.

“Some people think I'm too old for this,” Margaret says with a smile. “But the market keeps me young. Everybody knows my name here. Where else can you find that?”

title: Ask the Pharmacist
body:
Tomasz Nowak works as a bus mechanic in Cardiff. On Wednesday morning, he woke up with a sore throat and a runny nose. He didn't want to wait for an appointment with his GP, so at lunchtime he went to a pharmacy on Queen Street.

“Good afternoon. How can I help?” asked the pharmacist, a woman with glasses and a friendly Welsh accent.
“I've got a terrible sore throat, and my nose won't stop running.”
“How long have you had it?”
“Since yesterday evening.”
“Have you got a temperature?”
“I don't think so. I feel tired, but not hot.”
“Are you taking any other medicine at the moment? And are you allergic to anything?”
“No, nothing.”

The pharmacist nodded. “It sounds like a common cold. You don't need antibiotics, because they don't work against colds. Try these throat lozenges. Suck one every three hours. You can also take paracetamol for the pain, two tablets up to four times a day. And drink lots of water and hot tea with honey.”
“What about my nose?”
“This nasal spray will help. But don't use it for more than seven days.”

Everything cost eight pounds forty. “If you don't feel better in a week, or if you get a high temperature, go and see your GP,” she said.

Tomasz thanked her and went back to work with a pocket full of lozenges.

title: Popcorn and a Root Canal
body:
On Saturday evening, Kevin Park was eating popcorn in front of the TV in his apartment in Seattle when he felt a sharp pain in a back tooth. At first he ignored it. He took two painkillers and went to bed. But at three in the morning, he woke up. The pain was much worse, and the left side of his face was swollen.

His regular dentist's office was closed until Monday. Kevin searched online and found an emergency dental clinic that was open on weekends. He called at eight o'clock. “We can see you at ten,” said the receptionist. “Please bring your insurance card.”

At the clinic, Dr. Alvarez took an X-ray. “You have an infection under this tooth,” she said. “That's why it hurts so much. You need a root canal.”

Kevin was scared, but the dentist was very gentle. She gave him an injection, and after a few minutes he couldn't feel anything. The treatment took about an hour. Kevin also got a prescription for antibiotics.

His insurance paid for most of it, but he still paid three hundred dollars. On the way home, his mouth was numb and he couldn't smile properly.

That evening, his roommate offered him some popcorn. “No, thanks,” said Kevin. “I'm going to have soup.”

title: A Box for Melbourne
body:
Orla Byrne's younger sister, Saoirse, moved to Melbourne two years ago for work. In March, Saoirse was turning thirty, and Orla wanted to send her a birthday parcel from home.

Over two weeks, she slowly filled a shoebox. She put in three boxes of Irish tea, a few packets of cheese and onion crisps, a bar of chocolate, a framed photo of the two of them as children, and a card from their parents. Saoirse always complained that the tea in Australia tasted of nothing.

On a Monday morning, Orla took the parcel to the post office in Limerick. There was a short queue. When it was her turn, the woman behind the counter weighed the box. “Two point one kilos,” she said. “Where's it going?”
“Australia. It's a birthday present. It has to arrive before the fourteenth.”
“Then I'd send it express. It takes about a week, and you can track it online. Standard post can take three weeks or more.”

Orla also had to fill in a customs form. She wrote down everything in the box and its value. “No meat or fresh fruit?” asked the woman. “Australia is very strict.”
“Just tea, crisps and chocolate.”

Express cost almost seventy euro, more than the presents. But eight days later, Orla got a video call. Saoirse was holding a cup of tea and crying happily.

On Saturday, her phone rang. “Hello, this is TTC Lost and Found. We think we have your backpack.” A cleaner found it on the train at the end of the line and handed it in.

Fatima went to Bay Station the same afternoon. She showed her ID and described the backpack: dark grey, with a small maple leaf patch on the front. The man behind the desk brought it out. Everything was still inside, even her lunch box.

“Someone is very honest,” she said.

title: That Terrible Noise
body:
For two weeks, Tanya Brooks's car made a terrible noise. Every time she stopped at a red light in Columbus, the brakes squeaked loudly. People on the sidewalk turned and looked. Her teenage son pulled his hood over his face. “Mom, it's so embarrassing,” he said.

“My brakes squeak every time I stop. It's getting worse.”
“Okay. Let's take a look.”

Luis drove the car around the block and then put it up on the lift. After ten minutes, he called her over.
“See this? Your brake pads are almost completely worn out. This little metal piece is touching the rotor, and that's the noise. It's a warning.”
“Is it dangerous?”
“Not yet. But if you wait, it's going to damage the rotors, and that's much more expensive.”
“How much is it going to cost?”
“New front pads, parts and labor, about two hundred and twenty dollars. I can do it today. Come back at four.”

Tanya took the bus to work. At four o'clock, her car was ready. On the drive home, she stopped at every light. Silence. Her son smiled. “Finally.”

title: A Stone near Wanaka

“Great, that helps. The roads here are narrow, and there are lots of one-lane bridges. And in winter, there's sometimes ice in the mornings, so drive slowly.”

Nikau offered them full insurance for an extra twenty-five dollars a day. Daniel wanted to save money, but Wei Ling said yes. Nikau also gave them snow chains, just in case.

In the car park, they walked around the small white car and took photos of every scratch. The fuel tank was full. “Please bring it back with a full tank,” Nikau said, “or we charge you for the petrol.”

On the fourth day, near Wanaka, a stone flew up from a truck and cracked the windscreen. Daniel looked at Wei Ling. She smiled. “Aren't you happy we took the full insurance?”

“Excuse me,” she said. “I'm sorry, but this isn't what I ordered. I asked for the bean burger.”
Tyler's face went red. “Oh no, I'm so sorry! I'll fix that right away.”

The others started eating, and Aaliyah sipped her iced tea and waited. Ten minutes later, the manager came to the table with the right burger.
“I apologize for the mistake,” she said. “It's a crazy night. Your meal is on the house, and dessert is on us for the whole table.”

The peach cobbler was the best Aaliyah had ever eaten. When they paid, they left Tyler a good tip anyway. “Everyone has bad nights,” said Aaliyah.

title: The 7.42 to London Victoria

“This is a customer announcement. We are sorry to announce that the 7.42 service to London Victoria has been cancelled. This is due to a signal failure near Haywards Heath. The next train to London Victoria will be the 8.12, calling at Haywards Heath, Gatwick Airport, Clapham Junction and London Victoria. We apologise for any inconvenience.”

Kwame Asante sighed. He was standing on platform 4 at Brighton station with hundreds of other commuters. It was raining, and he had an important meeting at half past nine. He texted his manager.

The 8.12 was very crowded. Kwame didn't get a seat, so he stood in the corridor next to a man with a bicycle. He read his notes for the meeting on his phone.

The train arrived at Victoria at 9.25. Kwame ran to the Tube and got to the office at 9.50, just in time. Later that day, he filled in an online form to get some of his ticket money back. “At least I'll get a free coffee out of it,” he thought.

title: A Suit Somewhere in London
body:
Mateo Ricci flew from Rome to Vancouver for his sister's wedding. The journey was long: first a flight to London, then nine and a half hours over the Atlantic and across Canada. When he finally landed, he was tired but happy.

At the baggage carousel, he waited and waited. Hundreds of suitcases came out, but not his. After forty minutes, the carousel stopped. Mateo was the last passenger standing there.

He went to the baggage service desk. A woman named Kim looked at his boarding pass and typed on her computer. “I'm sorry,” she said. “Your suitcase is still in London. It missed the connection.”
“But my suit for the wedding is in it! The wedding is on Saturday.”
“Don't worry. It's going to come on tomorrow's flight, and we'll deliver it to your hotel.”

Kim filled in a report with him and gave him a reference number. She also gave him a small bag with a toothbrush, toothpaste and a T-shirt. “Keep your receipts if you need to buy anything,” she said. “The airline will pay you back.”

The next day, Mateo bought a shirt and some socks. He waited all evening, but nobody came. On Friday morning, he called the airline, and at last the suitcase arrived at reception.

On Saturday, he stood next to his sister in his own suit. Nobody knew about his adventure.

title: One Centimetre to Spare
body:
Zara and Liam had the same sofa for eight years. They bought it second-hand when they were students, and now it was old, saggy and stained. When you sat on it, you could feel a spring in your back. One Saturday, Liam's cousin sat on it and nearly disappeared. That was the moment they decided to buy a new one.

The next weekend, they drove to a big furniture store on the edge of Brisbane. There were hundreds of sofas, and they sat on more than twenty. Liam wanted a dark brown leather one. “It looks expensive, and it's easy to clean,” he said.
“Leather is terrible in a Brisbane summer,” said Zara. “Your legs stick to it.”

In the end, they agreed on a three-seater in green fabric, with deep cushions and wooden legs. It was soft, comfortable and big enough for both of them to lie on. It cost $1,600, plus $90 for delivery.

“Have you measured your doorway?” asked the sales assistant. They looked at each other. They hadn't.

On delivery day, the two men couldn't get the sofa through the front door. Zara held her breath. Then one of them smiled, took out a screwdriver and took the legs off. The sofa went through with one centimetre to spare.

That night, they watched a film on their new sofa and fell asleep before the end.

title: Red Frames
body:
For a few months, Bernie Kelly had headaches almost every evening. She loved reading and was in a book club in Cork, but after twenty minutes with a book, her eyes felt tired and her head hurt. She blamed her job, the weather and too much coffee.

One evening, her daughter Róisín watched her reading. Bernie was holding the book very far away from her face. “Mam,” Róisín laughed, “your arms aren't long enough any more. You need glasses!”

Bernie had never worn glasses in her life. But she booked an eye test at an optician's on Patrick Street. The optician, a young man called Eoin, asked her lots of questions. Then she read letters on a chart on the wall, first big, then smaller and smaller. He also tested her eyes with bright lights and different lenses.

“Your eyes are healthy,” he said, “but you're long-sighted. That's very normal after forty. You can see things far away clearly, but not things close to you. Reading glasses will help with the headaches.”

Choosing the frames took longer than the eye test. Bernie tried on at least fifteen pairs. In the end, she chose red ones. “If I'm going to wear glasses,” she said, “I want people to notice them.”

A week later, she picked them up. That evening, she read for two hours. No headache.

title: Friday Night at the Movies
body:
Marisol and Jenna met outside a movie theater in downtown Portland at seven o'clock on Friday. They didn't buy tickets online because they couldn't decide what to see. They stood in front of the big screen with the showtimes.

“What about The Silent House?” said Jenna. “It's a horror movie. Everyone says it's the scariest film of the year.”
“No way,” said Marisol. “The last time we watched a horror movie, I didn't sleep for three nights. What about Love in Lisbon? It's a romantic comedy.”
Jenna made a face. “Romantic comedies are all the same. They meet, they fight, they kiss. The end.”
“Okay, okay. What about the new space movie? It's longer, almost three hours, but the reviews are great.”
“Three hours? I have to get up early tomorrow. But fine.”

In the end, they agreed on the space movie. But at the ticket desk, the young man shook his head. “Sorry, that one's sold out. The only movie with seats left is Captain Penguin. It's animated. It starts in five minutes.”

Marisol and Jenna looked at each other and laughed. They bought two tickets, a huge bucket of popcorn and two sodas.

The theater was full of kids and parents. Ninety minutes later, Marisol and Jenna came out with red eyes. “That was the best movie I've seen all year,” said Jenna. “Don't tell anyone.”

title: Biscuit Goes to the Vet
body:
Last Tuesday our dog Biscuit didn't want his breakfast. That was strange, because Biscuit is a golden retriever and he usually eats everything, even my socks. He was lying in his bed, and he didn't wag his tail when my little brother Mateo called him.

Mom phoned the animal clinic, and the receptionist told us to come at eleven. We put Biscuit in the back of the car. Mateo held his paw the whole way.

The vet was Dr. Patel. She checked Biscuit's eyes, his ears and his stomach. When she touched his stomach, he cried a little. “I think he has eaten something bad,” she said. “Has he been in the garbage?”

Mom looked at me. On Sunday I forgot to close the garbage can after our barbecue. There were chicken bones in it.

Dr. Patel took an X-ray. Luckily, the bones were small and they weren't stuck. She gave Biscuit an injection for the pain and some medicine for five days. He had to eat only rice and boiled chicken for a week.

The bill was $240. I felt terrible, so I gave Mom twenty dollars from my birthday money.

Biscuit is much better now. He's running around the yard again, and I always close the garbage can.

title: A Card That Opens Doors

Juliana borrowed three easy readers and two films with English subtitles. On Wednesday she went to the conversation circle. There were people from Syria, Vietnam and Colombia, and they talked about their favourite food.

title: Doctor's Orders

The first week was hard. My legs hurt, and on Thursday I nearly stayed at home. But Kofi always remembered my name and asked how I was. Slowly it got easier.

title: A New Visa for Anish

Anish came to Melbourne from Kathmandu two years ago to study nursing. In March he got some bad news: he had failed one subject, so he needed an extra semester. His student visa was going to end in July, before his course finished.

He clicked “Submit”. A few minutes later an email arrived. It said he had a bridging visa, so he could stay in Australia legally while he waited for a decision.

The next eight weeks were the longest of his life. Every morning he checked his emails before breakfast.

Finally, in June, the message came: his visa was granted until next March. Anish called his mum in Nepal straight away. Then he started studying for his exam.

title: Everything Must Go

The drum kit was the most popular thing. Three teenagers wanted it, and a girl called Ruby bought it for $150. The baseball cards went to a collector for $80.

title: Sunflowers on Camden Street
body:
Ciarán met Leah in February at a pub quiz in Dublin. They had their first date a week later, and by April they were going out together. Then Leah mentioned her birthday. It was on Saturday.

Ciarán was nervous. He has never been good at presents. He decided to buy flowers, but he didn't know anything about them.

“Ah, a new girlfriend,” she said with a smile. “Then no red roses. Red roses are too serious. What does she like?”

Leah loved summer, the colour yellow and her bike, which was yellow too.

“Sunflowers,” said the florist. “Sunflowers are cheerful.”

She made a bouquet of five big sunflowers with some small white flowers and wrapped it in brown paper. It cost €35, but it looked fantastic. She also gave him a tip: “Cut the stems a little every two days, and change the water.”

On Saturday Ciarán carried the flowers carefully on the bus. When Leah opened the door, she laughed. “How did you know?” she said. “They're my favourite.”

He didn't tell her about the florist.

title: Waiting for the Number 23
body:
Mei moved to Edinburgh in September. Every morning she waited for the number 23 bus in Morningside, and every morning the same man was there: an older gentleman in a flat cap with a small brown dog.

For three weeks they only nodded at each other. Then one wet Tuesday he spoke.

“Dreich today, isn't it?”
“Sorry?” said Mei.
“Dreich. It's a Scottish word. It means grey, cold and wet, all at the same time.”
Mei laughed. “Then it's been dreich every day since I arrived!”
“Ah, you're new. Where are you from?”
“Singapore. It's much warmer there. I've never needed a winter coat before.”
“Well, you'll need one here. I'm Hamish, by the way, and this is Bonnie. We live at number 14.”
“I'm Mei. I'm at number 9, on the top floor.”

The bus was late, as usual, so they kept chatting. Hamish told her about the best chip shop in the area and the farmers' market on Saturdays.

When the bus finally came, Hamish didn't get on. “I only come for the chat,” he said with a wink. “Bonnie and I walk home now.”

The next morning it was dreich again. Mei smiled. Now she knew the word, and she had a neighbour.

title: Finally, the Rockies
body:
Gordon and Rosa Fraser both retired last year. Gordon was a mechanic, and Rosa was a nurse at the hospital in Halifax. For forty years they talked about one trip: the Rocky Mountains. They have travelled to Florida and to Portugal, but they have never seen the west of their own country.

Chantal showed them the cabins for two. They were small, with a real bed and a private bathroom. The windows were huge.

In the end they made a plan. They were going to fly to Toronto, take the train to Jasper and then rent a car. They were going to spend three nights in Banff and visit Lake Louise.

title: Two Wheels in Davis
body:
When Diego started his PhD at UC Davis in August, he didn't own a bike. He came from Los Angeles, where everybody drives. But in Davis, everyone cycles: students, professors, kids, even grandparents. There are bike lanes on almost every street.

For the first week, Diego walked everywhere. It was over 100 degrees, and the campus was huge. He was always late and always hot.

On Saturday he went to a bike shop downtown. The owner, a woman in her sixties called Barb, asked him three questions. “How far do you ride? Do you need to carry things? How much can you spend?”

Diego wanted something simple and cheap. Barb showed him a used blue commuter bike with a basket for $280. A new one was $650. “The used one is older, but it's just as good,” she said. “I checked it myself.”

Diego also bought a helmet, lights and a strong lock. “Bike theft is the biggest crime in this town,” Barb told him. “Always lock it to something.”

The next Monday, Diego rode to campus in twelve minutes. Hundreds of students were riding past him, and nobody crashed. For the first time, he felt like a real Davis student.

Two weeks later, his friend's bike was stolen. Diego bought a second lock.

title: Noah and the Lambs

Noah was ten, and he lived in an apartment on the fourteenth floor in central Auckland. He had never touched a sheep, a cow or even a chicken. So in the September school holidays, his parents sent him to stay with Aunty Mere on her farm near Geraldine, in Canterbury.

He also learned to collect eggs, and Kevin chased him twice.

When his parents came to pick him up, Noah didn't want to leave. “Can I come back in the summer?” he asked.

title: The Night the Lights Went Out
body:
It was a Tuesday in January, and it was minus thirty outside. Priya was cooking dal, her husband Arjun was helping their son Dev with his math homework, and the TV was on. Then, at ten past six, everything went black.

“Mom!” shouted Dev. “I can't see anything!”

Arjun turned on the flashlight on his phone. Priya looked out of the window. The whole street was dark. A heavy snowstorm was knocking down power lines all over Winnipeg.

The house got colder quickly, because the furnace needs electricity. Priya found some candles in a drawer and lit them. Arjun brought every blanket in the house. They put on their winter coats and sat close together on the sofa.

The dal was only half cooked, so they ate crackers, cheese and cold apples for dinner. Then Arjun told stories about his childhood in Punjab, where it never snowed. Dev laughed so much that he forgot to be scared.

At nine o'clock their neighbour, Mrs. Kowalski, knocked on the door with a thermos of hot chocolate. “I've lived here for fifty years,” she said. “This happens. Don't worry.”

The power came back at half past eleven. Dev was already asleep under four blankets. Nobody finished the homework.

title: Thirty Chairs in the Garden

In the evening my uncle played the fiddle, and we danced on the grass until it got dark. Then we lit candles in jam jars all around the garden.

They borrowed a tent, sleeping bags and a little gas stove from Hannah's brother. They reserved a campsite online and drove up on Friday afternoon.

In the evening they swam in the lake. The water was cold and clear, and the cliffs around it were beautiful in the sunset. Then they cooked hot dogs and made s'mores over the campfire.

At night it was very dark and very quiet. Hannah heard something outside and woke Kenji. “It's a bear!” she whispered. Kenji opened the tent slowly and turned on his flashlight. It was a raccoon, eating their bag of marshmallows.

body:
For two months the fourth bedroom in our flat in Newtown was empty. Lily, Jack and I advertised it online, and twelve people came to look at it. We chose Ana, a 27-year-old physio from Portugal. She seemed friendly and tidy, and she laughed at Jack's terrible jokes.

Ana moved in on a hot Saturday in February. She arrived in an Uber with two suitcases, a surfboard and a large plant. That was all.

“Is that everything?” asked Lily.
“Yes,” said Ana. “I like to travel light.”

We helped her carry her things upstairs. Then we showed her the house rules on the fridge: rubbish goes out on Tuesday night, everyone cleans the bathroom once a month, and no loud music after eleven. We also have a kitty for milk, bread and toilet paper. Everyone puts in $10 a week.

Ana read the list carefully. Then she took a pen and added one more rule: “Sunday dinner together.”

That first Sunday she cooked bacalhau, a Portuguese dish with salted cod and potatoes. Jack, who usually eats two-minute noodles, had three plates.

Now it's July, and we have had dinner together every Sunday. It's the best rule on the fridge.

title: Water Under the Door
body:
On Thursday morning Callum put a load of towels in the washing machine, pressed start and left for work. His girlfriend, Esme, was already at the university. Their flat in Glasgow was empty.

At half past eleven his phone rang. It was Mrs Lennox, the old lady in the flat downstairs.

“Callum, son, there's water coming through my kitchen ceiling!”

Callum ran to the subway and was home in twenty minutes. When he opened the front door, his socks got wet straight away. There was water all over the kitchen floor.

He switched the machine off and turned off the water under the sink. Then he got every towel from the cupboard and started mopping.

Downstairs, Mrs Lennox had a bucket on her kitchen table. Brown water was dripping into it from a crack in the ceiling. “Don't worry,” she said kindly. “It happened before, with the last tenants.”

Callum called the landlord, and a plumber came at four. The problem was an old hose at the back of the machine. It had a hole in it. The plumber changed it in ten minutes.

That evening Callum and Esme took Mrs Lennox a big box of chocolates and some flowers. Now they never leave the washing machine on when they go out.

title: Two Weeks of Early Mornings
body:
Monday
Today was the first day of my work experience. Everyone in Year 10 does two weeks in a real job. I chose a small bakery near the cathedral in Norwich, because I love baking. I had to be there at six. I've never got up so early in my life.

The owner, Rachel, gave me an apron and a hairnet. I looked ridiculous. My first job was weighing flour for the sourdough.

Wednesday
I learned how to shape loaves. It's harder than it looks. My first loaf was flat like a pancake. My second one was much better.

Friday
I served customers for the first time. A man asked for a “bloomer”, and I didn't know what it was. (It's a big white loaf.) I also dropped a tray of cheese scones, but Rachel said everybody does that once.

Second Wednesday
I made the cinnamon rolls on my own today, from the dough to the icing. We sold all forty before ten o'clock!

Last Friday
I was sad to leave. Rachel gave me a reference for my CV and a bag of warm croissants for my family. She said I can work on Saturdays in the summer holidays, and she's going to pay me. I'm definitely going to say yes.

title: How a Sitcom Taught Me English
body:
When I moved from Medellín to Houston three years ago, I could say “hello”, “thank you” and “one coffee, please”. That was all. I got a job in the kitchen of a Mexican restaurant, where everybody spoke Spanish, so my English didn't get better.

Then my roommate showed me a sitcom called Engine House 6. It's about a group of firefighters in a small town in Ohio. I watched the first episode with Spanish subtitles and laughed a lot.

After a month I switched to English subtitles. It was much harder. I paused every two minutes and wrote new words in a notebook: “rookie”, “no way”, “give me a break”. I repeated the jokes out loud.

After six months I turned the subtitles off. I didn't understand everything, but I understood the story.

The show helped me in real life too. One day a customer said, “Are you kidding me?” and I knew exactly what she meant. My manager noticed my English and moved me to the front of the restaurant. Now I'm a server, and I get better tips.

I've watched all seven seasons twice. Next month I'm going to start an English class at the community college. But I'm not going to stop watching Engine House 6.

title: One Size Too Small
body:
Chloe wanted to run the City-Bay Fun Run in Adelaide in September. It's twelve kilometres, from the city to the beach at Glenelg. Her old runners were five years old and had a hole in the toe, so she needed new ones.

She found a bright orange pair online, 30% off. They were $149 instead of $210. She ordered her usual size, and they arrived three days later.

Chloe tried them on straight away. They looked great, but they were too small. After ten minutes her feet hurt.

She checked the website. Returns were free within thirty days, as long as the shoes were unworn and in the original box. Luckily she only wore them inside. She filled in a form online and printed a label. The next day she took the parcel to the post office.

But the orange ones in a bigger size were sold out. So on Saturday she went to a running shop in the city. A young man watched her run on a treadmill and explained that her feet roll in when she runs. He recommended a different pair, half a size bigger.

They were blue and more expensive, but very comfortable. A week later her refund arrived. And in September, Chloe finished the fun run in 68 minutes.

title: Three Days on the Katy Trail
body:
Lauren's dad, Rick, turned sixty last spring. For his birthday she gave him an unusual present: a three-day bike trip with her on the Katy Trail in Missouri. The trail is an old railroad line, and for a long way it follows the Missouri River. It's flat and quiet, with no cars.

They started in St. Charles on a sunny Friday in October. Their plan was to ride about forty miles a day and sleep in small bed and breakfasts in old river towns.

The first day was easy. The trees were red and gold, and they stopped often for photos. In the afternoon they saw a bald eagle above the river. Rick was so excited that he nearly rode into a bush.

The second day was harder. It rained all morning, and the trail turned to mud. Lauren got a flat tire near Hermann, and they fixed it under a bridge. In the evening they ate the best pie of their lives at a little café.

On the third day the sun came back. Their legs were sore, but they rode faster than before. At four o'clock they arrived in Jefferson City, where Lauren's mom was waiting with the car.

“That was the best present I've ever had,” said Rick. “Next year, the whole trail?”

title: Just Popping Out for Croissants
body:
Freddie lives alone in a top-floor flat in Kemptown, Brighton. At eight o'clock last Sunday morning, he wanted fresh croissants. He put on his tracksuit, took his wallet and walked to the bakery at the end of the street.

When he came back, he put his hand in his pocket for his keys. Nothing. He checked his other pocket. Nothing. He walked back to the bakery, looking at the pavement, but the keys weren't there either.

Freddie didn't panic at first. His landlord had a spare key. He called him, but the landlord was on holiday in Spain. His sister in Hove also had a key, but she wasn't answering. It was Sunday morning, after all.

So he sat on the front steps and ate a croissant. Then another one.

At half past nine he looked online for a locksmith. The first one wanted £180 because it was Sunday. The second didn't answer.

Then his neighbour, Mrs Ahmed, came out with her dog. “Locked out?” she asked. “Your sister gave me a key last year, for emergencies. Don't you remember?”

Freddie didn't remember. But five minutes later he was inside, and Mrs Ahmed had the last croissant.

On Monday morning the woman at the bakery waved at him. “Are these yours?” She found them in the bread basket.

title: Mulled Wine and Snow in Edinburgh
body:
Lucas grew up in Recife, in the north of Brazil, where December is hot and sunny. Last winter he visited his old university friend Isla in Edinburgh for a week. On his second evening, she took him to the Christmas market in Princes Street Gardens.

It was only half past four, but it was already dark. Thousands of tiny lights hung above the wooden stalls, and a huge Ferris wheel turned slowly next to the castle. Lucas was wearing two jumpers under his coat, but he was still shivering.

“You need something warm,” Isla said, and she bought him a cup of mulled wine. It was hot and sweet and smelled of cinnamon. Then they shared a bag of roasted chestnuts and a sausage roll. The food was simpler than at home, but in the cold it tasted wonderful.

They walked past stalls with knitted hats, handmade candles and Christmas decorations. Lucas bought a tartan scarf for his mother. At one stall, a man was playing the bagpipes, and some children were dancing in front of him.

Later it started to snow. Lucas had never seen snow before. He stood still and held out his hands like a little boy.

“This is the best Christmas present ever,” he said. Isla laughed and took a photo of him.

title: Grandpa's First Chicago Winter
body:
For her history project, Maya had to interview an older person in her family. She chose her grandpa, Luis. On Saturday afternoon she sat at his kitchen table in Chicago with her notebook.

Maya: Where did you grow up, Grandpa?
Grandpa: In a small town in Puerto Rico, near the sea. We were poor, but I was happy. I swam every day after school.
Maya: Why did you leave?
Grandpa: When I was nineteen, my uncle found me a job in a factory here. I was nervous, but I wanted to earn money for my family.
Maya: What was the hardest thing?
Grandpa: The winter! I arrived in November with one thin jacket. On my first morning, I was walking to the bus stop when the wind nearly knocked me over. I never felt cold like that again.
Maya: Did you speak English?
Grandpa: Only a little. A kind neighbor taught me in the evenings. I paid her with my mother's recipes for rice and beans.

Maya laughed. Then Grandpa opened a drawer and took out an old black-and-white photo. It showed a young man in a suit outside a factory gate.

“That's me,” he said proudly. “My first paycheck day.”

Maya got an A for her project. She put a copy of the photo on the cover.

title: My First Match at St James' Park
body:
Saturday 14 October

Dear Diary,
Today was the best day of my life! Dad finally took me to see Newcastle United at St James' Park. He bought the tickets for my eleventh birthday, and I've waited three weeks for this day.

We took the Metro into the city centre. The train was full of fans in black-and-white shirts, and they were already singing. I was wearing my new scarf and Dad's old woolly hat.

The stadium was enormous. When I looked down at the pitch from our seats, the grass looked greener than on TV. More than fifty thousand people were there! Before kick-off, everybody stood up and sang together. I didn't know the words, so I just clapped.

The first half was boring because nobody scored. At half-time Dad bought me a pie and a hot chocolate. Then, in the seventy-eighth minute, our striker headed the ball into the net. The noise was incredible. A man next to us hugged Dad, and I screamed until my throat hurt.

We won 1-0. On the way home I fell asleep on the Metro. Dad says we can go again in the spring. I can't wait!

title: Priya's First Babysitting Night
body:
Priya was a second-year student at the University of Toronto, and she needed extra money for her rent. Her neighbour, Mrs. Martin, asked her to babysit on Friday evening.

“The kids are easy,” Mrs. Martin said. “Leo is six and Zoe is three. Dinner is in the fridge, and bedtime is at eight.”

At first, everything went well. Priya heated up the pasta, and the children ate it all. After dinner they built a tower with blocks and coloured pictures of dinosaurs.

Then the problems started. Zoe refused to put on her pyjamas. Leo wanted three bedtime stories, not one. While Priya was reading the second story, Zoe disappeared. Priya searched the bathroom, the kitchen and the hallway. Her heart was beating fast.

Finally she heard a giggle from the laundry basket. Zoe was hiding under a pile of towels!

By nine o'clock both children were asleep. Priya sat on the sofa, completely exhausted. She sent a message to her mom: “Babysitting is harder than my exams!”

When the Martins came home at eleven, the house was quiet and tidy. Mrs. Martin paid her sixty dollars and asked, “Can you come again next Friday?”

Priya smiled and said yes.

Hi Siobhán,

Guess what? I passed my A2 English exam! The results came this morning, and I was so happy that I danced in the hotel kitchen.

Do you remember how nervous I was last month? The night before the exam, I couldn't sleep at all. I got up at six, drank two cups of strong tea and took the bus into Cork city centre. The exam centre was in an old building near the river.

The reading and writing part was first. It was easier than I expected, because we practised those kinds of texts so often in your class. Then came the listening. One recording was about a train timetable, and the speaker talked very fast. I didn't understand everything, so I guessed some answers.

The speaking test was in the afternoon. My partner was a young man from Brazil. The examiner showed us photos of holidays, and we discussed them together. My hands were shaking at the start, but after a minute I relaxed.

I got 132 points, and I needed 120 to pass. Thank you for your patience every Tuesday evening. Next year I'm going to try the B1 exam!

title: Tim Tams on Ward 7B
body:
Last Thursday my best mate, Tom, had an operation on his knee. He hurt it in March during a footy match, and the doctors decided it needed surgery. The day after the operation, I went to visit him at the Royal Brisbane Hospital.

I wasn't sure what to bring. In the end I bought some grapes, a car magazine and a packet of Tim Tams, his favourite biscuits. At reception, a friendly nurse showed me the way to Ward 7B.

Tom was lying in bed with a big bandage around his leg. He looked pale and tired, but he smiled when he saw the Tim Tams.

“The food here is terrible,” he whispered. “These are the best thing all week.”

We played cards for an hour and talked about our footy team. Tom told me that the operation went well. He has to use crutches for six weeks, and after that he needs physio twice a week. He was worried because he can't drive or go to work.

“Don't worry,” I said. “I'll drive you to physio. And I'll bring more Tim Tams.”

When visiting hours ended at eight, the nurse came to check his blood pressure. I promised to come back on Saturday with the rest of the team.

title: Falling Asleep in London, Waking Up in Scotland
body:
Every year Chloe flew from London to Inverness to visit her grandmother. This spring she decided to try something different: the Caledonian Sleeper, a night train from London to Scotland.

“It's better for the planet,” she told her friends, “and I don't have to be at the airport at five in the morning.”

The train left Euston station at quarter to nine in the evening. Chloe's cabin was tiny, with a narrow bed, a small sink and a window. There were soft towels and a little bag with soap and earplugs. She put her suitcase under the bed and went to the lounge car. There she ordered macaroni cheese and chatted to an old man from Aberdeen. He took this train every month and knew all the stations.

At about eleven Chloe went back to her cabin. The train rocked gently from side to side, and she fell asleep faster than she expected.

When she woke up, she opened the blind. Outside, there were mountains, lakes and a few sheep in the mist. It was the most beautiful view of her life, and she was still in bed! A steward brought her tea and a bacon roll.

The journey was longer than a flight, but Chloe arrived in Inverness relaxed and happy. She has already booked her ticket for the autumn.

title: Kenji's First Mardi Gras
body:
Kenji moved from Osaka to New Orleans in September for a job at a shipping company. In February his colleagues kept asking him the same question: “Are you ready for Mardi Gras?” Kenji wasn't sure what they meant.

On Saturday his coworker Denise invited him to watch a parade with her family on St. Charles Avenue. They arrived early because the best spots fill up fast. Families were already sitting on folding chairs and ladders, and people were cooking hot dogs on small grills.

When the parade started, Kenji couldn't believe his eyes. Huge colorful floats rolled slowly down the street, and the riders on them wore masks and glittery costumes. Brass bands played loud, happy music, and everyone danced on the sidewalk.

“Throw me something!” Denise's kids shouted. The riders threw plastic beads, cups and toys into the crowd. Kenji caught a long purple necklace with one hand. By the end of the day, he was wearing twelve of them.

Later, Denise's mother gave him a slice of king cake. Inside his piece he found a tiny plastic baby.

“That means you buy the next cake!” everybody laughed.

On Monday Kenji brought a king cake for the whole office.

title: A Note Under the Door
body:
Aroha works as a nurse at Wellington Hospital. Her shifts start at half past six in the morning, so she usually goes to bed at nine.

In June a young man moved into the flat above hers. He seemed friendly, but every night he played loud music until midnight. Sometimes Aroha heard him dragging furniture across the floor. She lay awake for hours, and at work she felt like a zombie.

After a week she wrote a note and pushed it under his door:

“Hi! I'm Aroha from Flat 3. I'm a nurse and I start work very early. Could you please keep the music down after nine? Thanks!”

The next evening someone knocked on her door. It was the young man, with a box of chocolates.

“I'm so sorry,” he said. “My name's Finn. I'm a DJ, and I practise for my gigs in the evenings. I had no idea the walls were so thin.”

They talked for a while. Finn promised to wear headphones after nine, and he bought a thick rug for his living room floor. Aroha gave him her phone number in case there was another problem.

Since then, the building has been quiet at night. Last month Finn even invited Aroha to one of his gigs on a Saturday, when she didn't have to work. She danced until two in the morning.

title: Spring Comes to Our Backyard
body:
In Winnipeg, winter is long. This year the snow covered our backyard from November until the middle of April. When it finally melted, the garden looked terrible. The grass was brown and flat, and there were broken branches everywhere.

On the first warm Saturday in May, Mom woke me up at eight. “Put on your old clothes, Mateo,” she said. “Today we're getting the garden ready.”

First we raked the dead leaves and picked up the branches. My little sister, Lucía, found a tennis ball that we lost last summer. Then Dad dug the vegetable beds while I pushed the wheelbarrow full of compost. My back hurt after an hour, but the sun was shining and the birds were singing.

After lunch we went to the garden centre and bought seeds and small plants: tomatoes, beans, lettuce and some sunflowers for Lucía. Mom says it's too early for tomatoes outside, so we left them on the kitchen windowsill. Last year a frost killed them in late May.

In the evening I was dirty and tired, but our backyard looked much better. Dad lit the barbecue for the first time this year, and we ate burgers outside in our jackets.

Next weekend I'm going to paint the fence. Mom promised to pay me twenty dollars.

title: Three Friends and One Big Rollercoaster
body:
Last July, Ashley, Marcus and Jenna drove two hours from Columbus to Cedar Point, a famous theme park on Lake Erie. They left at seven in the morning because they wanted to be at the gates when the park opened.

Marcus loved fast rides. Ashley liked them too, but Jenna was scared of heights. “I'll hold your bags,” she said. “That's my job today.”

The first ride was a huge wooden rollercoaster. The line took forty minutes, and Marcus talked about it the whole time. Ashley screamed from the top to the bottom, and when she got off, her legs were shaking.

At lunch they ate corn dogs and fries next to the lake. It was ninety degrees, so afterwards they went on a water ride. All three of them got completely soaked, and Jenna laughed more than anyone.

In the afternoon her friends finally convinced Jenna to try a small rollercoaster. She closed her eyes and held Ashley's hand tightly. After the ride she was smiling. “That was actually fun,” she said. “Can we go again?”

They stayed until the fireworks at ten. Jenna drove home while the other two slept. “Next year,” she told them the next morning, “I'm going on the big one.”

title: Three Bins and a Bag of Bottles
body:
When Arjun moved from Delhi to Parramatta in western Sydney, he found three wheelie bins behind his townhouse. One had a red lid, one had a yellow lid and one had a green lid. He had no idea which bin was for what.

On his first Monday, he put a big bag of rubbish into the yellow bin. That evening his neighbour, Bev, knocked on his door.

“Sorry, love,” she said, “but that bag goes in the red bin. Yellow is only for recycling.”

Then she explained the rules. Paper, cardboard, glass bottles, cans and hard plastic containers go in the yellow bin, loose, not in bags. Food scraps and general rubbish go in the red bin. The green bin is for grass, leaves and branches.

“And never put soft plastic in the yellow bin,” she added. “Take it to the supermarket instead.”

Bev also told him about bin night. The council collects the red bin every week, but the other two only every second week. You put them out on the street the night before.

Then she gave him one last tip: “Keep your drink bottles and cans. At the machine near the station, you get ten cents for each one.”

Last month Arjun took forty bottles there and got four dollars. He used it to buy Bev a coffee.

title: Dad's Victoria Sponge
body:
In June, a letter came home from Ruby's primary school in Bristol. The summer fair was on Saturday, and the school needed cakes for the cake stall. Ruby's mum was away for work, so her dad, Femi, said, “No problem. We'll bake one together.”

Femi had never baked a cake before. On Friday evening he found a recipe for a Victoria sponge online. It looked simple: butter, sugar, eggs, flour, jam and cream.

The first cake was a disaster. Femi forgot to set a timer, and when he opened the oven, the top was black. Ruby held her nose. “It smells like a bonfire, Dad.”

They started again. This time Ruby weighed the flour carefully, and Femi set two timers on his phone. The second cake came out golden, but it sank a little in the middle.

“Don't worry,” Ruby said. “We can hide it.” She spread raspberry jam and whipped cream between the two halves, then covered the top with strawberries and icing sugar.

At the fair the next day, their cake sat between beautiful cakes from other parents, and Femi felt nervous. But after ten minutes, a teacher bought the whole thing for the staff room.

“Best sponge I've had in years,” she told him on Monday.

title: Forty-Two People and One Flat
body:
Aoife got a new job in Dublin in January, and she needed a flat quickly. Her boyfriend, Rahul, was moving with her. Their budget was 1,900 euro a month, and they soon learned that this was not a lot in Dublin.

They found an advert for a one-bedroom flat in Phibsborough for 1,850 euro. The viewing was on Saturday at eleven. When they arrived at ten to eleven, there was already a queue down the street. Aoife counted forty-two people.

The letting agent let everyone in, in groups of ten. The flat was on the third floor, and there was no lift. The kitchen was tiny, and the bathroom had black mould in the corner. But the bedroom was bright, with a view of the canal.

“What do you think?” Rahul whispered.

“I think everyone here wants it,” Aoife whispered back.

The agent asked for references from their employers, three payslips and a deposit. Rahul had a folder with all the documents, and he gave it to her straight away. Many other people didn't have theirs.

They didn't get that flat. But two weeks later the same agent rang them. “You were so organised,” she said. “I have another flat for you, and it isn't advertised yet.”

They moved in on the first of March.

title: Jasmine's First Paycheck
body:
Jasmine finished college in May, and in June she started her first full-time job as a graphic designer in Atlanta. At the end of the month, her first paycheck arrived in her bank account: $2,600 after taxes.

For about ten minutes, she felt rich. She opened a shopping app and put a new laptop, three pairs of sneakers and a weekend in Miami into her cart. Then she called her aunt Denise, who works at a bank.

“Wait,” Aunt Denise said. “Before you buy anything, make a budget. Try the 50/30/20 rule.”

That evening, Jasmine sat at her kitchen table and wrote this in a notebook:

Needs (50%): $1,300 for rent, bills, groceries and gas
Wants (30%): $780 for eating out, movies, clothes and the gym
Savings (20%): $520 for an emergency fund and her student loan

She realized the laptop was not a need, and neither was Miami. She deleted most things from her cart but kept one pair of sneakers.

Three months later, her car broke down on the highway. The repair cost $700. Jasmine was stressed, but she didn't have to borrow any money. She paid for it from her emergency fund.

“Thanks, Aunt Denise,” she texted. “The budget saved me.”

title: Our Trip to Conwy Castle
body:
By Osian Jones, Year 6

Last Tuesday our class went on a trip to Conwy Castle in North Wales. We left school at half past eight on a big coach. The journey took an hour, and Mrs Hughes made us sing songs in Welsh the whole way.

When we arrived, it was raining, but nobody cared. The castle was enormous, with eight round towers and thick stone walls. Our guide, Gareth, told us that King Edward the First built it more than seven hundred years ago. It took only four years and about fifteen hundred workers.

First we visited the Great Hall. It doesn't have a roof any more, so the rain fell on our heads. Then we climbed a spiral staircase to the top of a tower. It was dark and slippery, and my friend Cerys held onto my jacket. From the top we could see the whole town, the river and the mountains.

At lunchtime we ate our packed lunches on a bench. Suddenly a huge seagull flew down and stole half of Dylan's cheese sandwich. Everybody screamed, and Dylan nearly cried.

In the gift shop I bought a small plastic knight for my brother. It was the best school trip ever, even with the rain and the seagull.

title: Snow Days in Queenstown
body:
Grace grew up in Auckland, where it never snows. So when her friend Hemi invited her on a ski trip to Queenstown in July, she was excited and a bit scared. Hemi had skied every winter since he was five.

They flew down on a Friday and rented a small apartment in town. The next morning they took the bus up to Coronet Peak. Grace hired skis, boots and a helmet. The boots were so heavy that she walked like a robot.

Hemi wanted to go straight to the top, but Grace booked a lesson for beginners. Her instructor, a cheerful woman from Canada, taught the group how to stop. “Make a pizza shape with your skis,” she said. Grace fell over eleven times that morning. Once she slid all the way down the slope on her back.

On the second day it was easier. Grace learned to turn, and she rode the chairlift for the first time. Her legs were shaking, but Hemi sat next to her and talked the whole time.

On the last afternoon, she skied down a whole green run without falling. Hemi was waiting at the bottom and clapped loudly.

That evening they drank hot chocolate by a fire. Grace's legs hurt, but she was already planning next winter.

title: Lunch at Grandma Pat's
body:
On the first Sunday of every month, my whole family goes to Grandma Pat's house in Leeds for lunch. There are usually twelve of us: my parents, my brother, two aunts, an uncle and five cousins. Grandma's kitchen is small, but somehow we all fit.

Last Sunday we arrived at one o'clock, and the house already smelled of roast beef. Grandma was wearing her old flowery apron. “Jade,” she said to me, “you're fifteen now. Today you're going to make the Yorkshire puddings.”

I was nervous. Grandma's Yorkshire puddings are famous in our family, and she never uses a recipe. She showed me how to mix flour, eggs and milk into a smooth batter. Then we poured it into a tin with very hot oil.

“Don't open the oven door,” she warned me. “Not even once.”

After twenty minutes I took them out. They were tall, golden and crispy. Uncle Steve, who always complains about something, ate four.

We had the beef with roast potatoes, carrots, peas and lots of gravy. For dessert there was apple crumble with custard. Afterwards the adults washed up, and the cousins played cards.

Before we left, Grandma gave me a little card. On it, in her neat handwriting, was her recipe. She wrote it down just for me.

title: A Cough Like a Seal
body:
At two o'clock on a Tuesday morning, Mei woke up to a strange sound. It came from the next room, where her son Noah was sleeping. He was two years old, and he had a cold that week. But this sounded different: a loud, barking cough, like a seal.

Mei ran into his room. Noah was sitting up and crying, and every time he breathed in, he made a high, whistling noise. She woke her husband, Ryan.

“His breathing isn't right,” she said.

Ryan called the nurse line on the back of their insurance card. The nurse listened to Noah over the phone. “It sounds like croup,” she said calmly. “Take him to the emergency room now. If his lips turn blue, call 911.”

They wrapped Noah in a blanket and drove through the empty streets of Denver. It was snowing, and Ryan opened the window a little. Strangely, the cold air helped, and Noah's breathing got easier.

At the children's hospital, a doctor examined him quickly. She gave Noah some medicine in a cup of juice and checked his oxygen. After an hour he was asleep in Mei's arms.

They got home at six, just as the sun was coming up. Ryan made coffee, and finally Mei cried too.

title: Saturdays with Bridie
body:
Last September, when Cian started Transition Year at his school in Galway, every student had to do some volunteering. Most of his friends chose the charity shop or the football club. Cian chose a nursing home near Salthill, because his own granny lived far away in Donegal and he missed her.

On his first Saturday, he was very nervous. He didn't know what to say to old people he didn't know. The manager, Eileen, gave him a simple job: serving tea and biscuits in the day room.

That's where he met Bridie. She was ninety-one and very small, and she wore bright red lipstick every day. When Cian brought her tea, she looked at him and said, “You're too thin. Have a biscuit yourself.”

After that, Cian sat with Bridie every week. She taught him to play rummy, and she won almost every game. She told him stories about dancing in Galway in the 1950s and about her first job in a hat shop. Cian showed her videos of her old street on his phone.

Transition Year ended in May, but Cian still goes to the nursing home every Saturday. Last month Bridie turned ninety-two. He brought her a red lipstick and a big box of biscuits, and she cried a little.

title: A Letter from Vancouver
body:
Dear Grandad,

I know you don't like emails, so here is a real letter with a real stamp! I've been in Vancouver for two months now, and I want to tell you about my exchange semester.

The university campus is huge. It's next to the sea, and on clear days I can see mountains with snow on top. My room in the student residence is small, but I share a kitchen with five students from Mexico, Korea, Germany and Canada. Last week we all cooked dinner together, and I made your shepherd's pie. Everyone loved it!

My classes are harder than at home in Sheffield. The professors expect us to speak in every seminar, and at first I was too shy. Now I'm getting more confident.

People here are very polite. They say “sorry” even more than we do in England! And everybody talks about the weather, just like you.

Last weekend my friend Ji-woo and I hired bikes and rode around Stanley Park. We saw a family of raccoons and a bald eagle in a tree.

I'm coming home in December, just before Christmas. Please save me a seat by the fire, and tell Gran I miss her cooking.

Lots of love,
Ellie

P.S. I've put a maple leaf in the envelope for you.

title: My Crazy Melbourne Weather Diary
body:
People say Melbourne can have four seasons in one day. Last week, I found out it's true. Here is my weather diary.

Monday: Hot and sunny, 34 degrees. I wore shorts and sandals to uni and bought an ice block at lunch.

Tuesday: Even hotter, 39 degrees. Then, at four o'clock, a cool change arrived. The wind suddenly turned, and the temperature fell by fifteen degrees in half an hour. I was shivering at the tram stop in my T-shirt.

Wednesday: Grey and windy. My umbrella blew inside out on Swanston Street, so I threw it in the bin.

Thursday: A huge storm. Thunder woke me up at 3 a.m., and hailstones as big as marbles hit the roof. In the morning there were white piles of ice on the footpath, like snow in summer! Some cars in our street had dents.

Friday: Beautiful again. Blue sky, 22 degrees, no wind. Everyone was outside in the parks.

Saturday: Foggy in the morning, sunny at lunchtime, rainy in the afternoon. I changed my clothes three times.

Sunday: I stayed home and checked the forecast. It says 35 degrees tomorrow, with storms in the evening. I've learned my lesson: I'm going to take a jumper, a new umbrella and sunscreen.

title: From the Sofa to the Finish Line
body:
Staff News, Clyde Insurance, Glasgow

In March, Kirsty from the accounts team sent an email to everyone in the office. Her little nephew spent three months at the Royal Hospital for Children last year, and she wanted to raise money for it. Her idea: a team of colleagues running the Glasgow 10K in June.

Twelve people signed up. Some, like Raj from IT, already ran every weekend. Others, like Brian from reception, never ran at all. “I get out of breath on the stairs,” Brian admitted.

The team trained together on Tuesday and Thursday evenings after work. They started slowly along the river, running for one minute and walking for two. Every week they ran a little further.

There were difficult moments. In April it rained for three weeks, and Oksana from marketing twisted her ankle. But she came back in May and ran faster than ever.

On race day, the whole team wore matching yellow T-shirts, and all twelve finished. Raj was the fastest, at forty-four minutes. Brian crossed the line after an hour and twenty minutes with his arms in the air, and the team cheered louder for him than for anyone.

Together they raised £6,350 for the hospital. Next year, Brian says, he's going to do the half marathon.

title: The Kettle That Stopped Boiling
body:
Three weeks ago, Hamid bought a new kettle from an electrical shop in the Bullring, Birmingham's big shopping centre. It cost thirty-five pounds. For two weeks it worked perfectly. Then, one morning, he switched it on and nothing happened.

Hamid wasn't happy. He drinks at least five cups of tea a day. He found the receipt in a drawer, put the kettle back in its box and took the bus into town.

At the customer service desk, a young woman called Sophie smiled at him.
“Hello. How can I help?”
“I bought this kettle three weeks ago, and it's stopped working.”
“Oh no. Have you got the receipt?”
“Yes, here it is.”
Sophie plugged the kettle in and pressed the switch. Nothing.
“You're right, it's faulty. Would you like a replacement or a refund?”
Hamid thought about it. “A refund, please. I think I'll try a different brand.”
“No problem. You bought it less than thirty days ago, so you get all your money back.”

Five minutes later, Hamid had his thirty-five pounds back on his card. On the way home, he bought a cheaper kettle in the supermarket for twenty pounds. He made a cup of tea the moment he got home, and the new kettle has worked perfectly ever since.
