title: A Very Wobbly Mug
body:
For her birthday, Kayla's best friend, Brooke, gave her a surprising present: two tickets for a beginners' pottery class in Portland. “No phones, no screens,” Brooke said. “Just us and some mud.”

The class was on a Wednesday evening in a small studio with big windows. The teacher, Rosa, had gray hair and clay on her apron. She showed the six students how to throw a ball of clay onto the center of the potter's wheel. Then she pressed her wet hands on it, and two minutes later there was a perfect bowl.

“It looks easy,” Kayla whispered.

It wasn't. When Kayla started her wheel, the clay flew off and hit the wall. On her second try, the clay stayed on the wheel, but her bowl got taller and thinner until it fell over.

Brooke was better. She made a small cup with straight sides, and Rosa said she had “good hands.”

By the end of the evening, Kayla had one finished piece: a very wobbly mug. She painted it blue and yellow. Rosa put everything in the kiln, a special oven that gets extremely hot.

A week later they picked up their work. Kayla's mug leaned to one side, but it didn't leak. Now she drinks her coffee from it every morning, and the two friends have signed up for a six-week course.

title: The Quarter Past One Bus
body:
Leila lives in Woodingdean, a village on the hill above Brighton. On Saturday night she went to her friend Grace's twentieth birthday party in a flat near the seafront. Before she left home, her dad said, “The last bus is at quarter past one. Don't miss it.”

The party was great. There was a DJ and a huge chocolate cake, and Leila danced with people from her college. At ten past one she looked at her phone and screamed. She grabbed her coat and ran down the street.

She arrived at the stop just in time to see the bus disappear around the corner.

Leila stood there alone. It was cold, and her phone battery was at eight per cent. A taxi app said a car cost twenty-five pounds, and she only had twelve. Walking home took over an hour, mostly along a dark road, and she didn't want to do that.

She took a deep breath and called her dad.

“I missed it,” she said quietly.

He didn't shout. He just said, “Go back inside where it's warm. I'll be there in fifteen minutes.”

Twenty minutes later, his old car stopped outside Grace's building. Her dad was wearing a coat over his pyjamas, and slippers on his feet. Leila hugged him.

“Next time,” he said with a smile, “leave at one.”

title: Biscuit Chooses Diego
body:
After two years of working from home in Austin, Diego felt lonely. He talked to his houseplants more than to people. So one Saturday in March, he drove to the animal shelter. His plan was simple: adopt a cute kitten.

A volunteer called Tasha showed him around. The kittens were adorable, but they were also very wild. One climbed up his leg, and another one bit his finger.

“Can I show you someone special?” Tasha asked.

In the last room, a big orange cat was sleeping on a blanket. His name was Biscuit, and he was seven years old. His owner moved into a care home and couldn't take him. Biscuit was at the shelter for five months because most people wanted younger cats.

Diego sat down on the floor. After a minute, Biscuit opened one eye, walked over slowly and climbed into his lap. Then he started purring.

“I think he's chosen you,” Tasha said.

Diego filled out the adoption form and paid a fee of fifty dollars. That included Biscuit's vaccinations and a microchip. On the way home he bought a litter box, a bag of food and a scratching post.

Now Biscuit sleeps on Diego's desk every day, right next to his laptop. Sometimes he walks across the keyboard during video calls, and Diego's coworkers love him.

title: Ninety-Nines by the Harbour
body:
Last summer, when I was seventeen, I got my first job at an ice-cream kiosk on the harbour in St Ives, Cornwall. I wanted to save money for driving lessons, and I liked the idea of working by the sea.

On my first morning, the owner, Mr Penrose, gave me a striped apron and showed me the twenty-four flavours. The most popular was Cornish clotted cream, but tourists also loved salted caramel. He taught me how to make a perfect scoop and how to push a chocolate flake into a cone. In Britain that's called a “ninety-nine.”

The first week was hard. My arm hurt from scooping, and I was slow with the till. Once I gave a man change for twenty pounds when he only gave me a tenner. Mr Penrose wasn't angry. “Everyone does it once,” he said.

In August there was a heatwave. The queue went all the way along the harbour, and we sold more than eight hundred ice creams in one day. I didn't have time for lunch, but the customers were friendly, and the tip jar was full by the evening.

By September I had saved nine hundred pounds, enough for twenty driving lessons. I passed my test in December. Mr Penrose has already asked me to come back next summer.

title: Grandpa Gets a Smartphone
body:
For his eightieth birthday, my grandpa, Ken, got his first smartphone from the family. His old phone was a tiny grey thing with buttons, and it could only make calls. Mum asked me to teach him how to use the new one, because I'm sixteen and “good with technology.”

Every Wednesday after school, I cycled to his house in Christchurch. The first lesson was a disaster. Grandpa pressed the screen too hard, and he kept taking photos of his own nose by accident. He also didn't understand why the phone needed a password.

“My old phone never asked me for a secret code,” he complained.

So we started slowly. I made the text bigger and put only four apps on the home screen: Phone, Messages, Camera and Weather. Every week he practised, and every week he got a bit faster.

In the fourth week, I showed him how to make a video call. His brother Bill lives in Scotland, and they last saw each other nine years ago. When Bill appeared on the screen, Grandpa went very quiet. Then they both started laughing, and they talked for an hour.

Now Grandpa sends me a message every morning. It usually says, “Good morning. Weather is fine. Love, Grandpa.” Yesterday he sent his first emoji: a thumbs-up.

title: Jollof, Tamales and a Texas Brisket
body:
When Mariana moved into her new apartment in Houston, she didn't know anyone in the building. So she put a note in the elevator: “Potluck dinner, Saturday 7 p.m., Apartment 4C. Bring a dish from home!”

She was worried that nobody was going to come. But at seven o'clock the doorbell rang, and it didn't stop ringing for half an hour. Eleven neighbors came, and every one of them carried a dish.

Mariana made tamales, like her grandmother in Monterrey. Linh from 2A brought Vietnamese spring rolls with peanut sauce. Mr. Okafor from 5B brought a huge pot of Nigerian jollof rice, and Ama, a nurse from Ghana, brought her own jollof rice too.

“Mine is better,” they both said at the same time, and everybody laughed. Of course, the guests had to taste both. Mariana secretly thought they were equally delicious.

The last guest was Earl, an old man from the first floor. He was born in Texas and has lived in the building for thirty years. He brought a smoked brisket that he cooked for twelve hours.

They ate on the sofa, on chairs and on the balcony. People shared recipes and stories about their home countries.

Before they left, the neighbors made a decision: a potluck every month, in a different apartment each time.

title: Mom's Note in My Wallet
body:
Before Jordan left Iowa for his first trip to New York City, his mom put a small piece of paper in his wallet. On it, she wrote his cousin's address in Brooklyn and her phone number. “Phones die,” she said. Jordan rolled his eyes.

On his second day, he went into Manhattan alone. He walked through Central Park, ate a giant slice of pizza and took hundreds of photos in Times Square. He was using his phone for everything: maps, subway times, music.

At six in the evening, the screen went black. The battery was dead, and his charger was at his cousin's apartment.

Suddenly the city felt enormous. Jordan had no idea which train to take. He walked for twenty minutes and got more lost.

Then he remembered the note. He took it out of his wallet and showed it to a woman selling hot dogs on the corner.

“Brooklyn? Easy,” she said. “Go down those stairs and take the F train. Get off at Seventh Avenue.”

On the platform, a kind older man checked the subway map with him. Forty minutes later, Jordan was ringing his cousin's doorbell.

That night he called his mom from his cousin's phone. “Thanks for the note,” he said. She didn't say “I told you so,” but he could hear her smiling.

title: Happy Birthday, Kevin!
body:
For weeks, Hannah planned a surprise party for her husband, Kwame, who was turning forty. She booked the back room of an Italian restaurant in Manchester's Northern Quarter and invited thirty friends in a secret group chat.

The first problem came on Tuesday. Kwame picked up her phone to check the weather, and a message appeared on the screen: “What time is the party on Saturday?” Hannah's heart stopped. “Oh, that's Jess's leaving party at work,” she said quickly. Kwame shrugged.

On Saturday morning, she went to collect the cake. The box was beautiful, but when she opened it, the icing said “Happy 40th, Kevin!” The baker apologised, but there was no time to make a new one.

The worst problem came at six. Kwame was on the sofa in his tracksuit. “I'm really tired,” he said. “Let's just get a takeaway tonight.”

Hannah panicked and texted his brother, Kofi. Ten minutes later Kofi phoned: “Come for one quick drink, mate. I've had a terrible week.” Kwame sighed, but he put on a shirt.

At eight o'clock he walked into the restaurant, and thirty people shouted, “Surprise!” Kwame's mouth fell open. Then he hugged Hannah for a long time.

When he saw the cake, he laughed even more. “From now on,” he said, “you can all call me Kevin.”

title: Red Mud and Fresh Eggs
body:
Last August, Sara and her husband, Omar, took their children on a farm holiday instead of a hotel. Ethan was eight and Ava was five, and they knew cows only from TV. The family drove from Montreal to Prince Edward Island, almost twelve hours with stops.

The farm belonged to the MacDonald family. It had potato fields, a red barn, twenty cows, some pigs and lots of chickens. The ground on the island is red, and after the first day the children's socks were red too.

Every morning started at seven. Mrs. MacDonald gave the children a basket, and they collected eggs from the henhouse. Ava was scared of the chickens at first, but by Wednesday she knew all their names. Ethan helped Mr. MacDonald feed the calves. One calf licked his face, and he laughed for five minutes.

In the afternoons they went to the beach. On Thursday it rained, so they baked bread in the farmhouse kitchen.

On the last evening, the family ate lobster rolls and corn on the cob at a long table outside while the sun went down over the fields.

“Can we live here?” Ava asked.

In the car the next morning, both children cried. Now Ethan wants to be a farmer, and Ava has a photo of her favourite hen on her bedroom wall.
